title: Chillianwala, 1849
hook: a battle in thick scrub near the Jhelum, fought into the dark, and a Sikh army that would not give way

segments.voice: Yesterday, Multan rose, and your line was the spark. Today, the fire it started reaches a field by a river.

Late afternoon, near the river Jhelum. The ground ahead is thick with thorny scrub, so dense a soldier can barely see the man beside him. Somewhere in it waits the Sikh army under Sher Singh Attariwala. The British commander, Lord Gough, had meant to wait for morning. Instead, with the light already going, he orders the attack. Regiments push into the thorns, and guns open up from places nobody can see.
screen: `THORNY SCRUB BY THE JHELUM.` → `THE LIGHT IS GOING.` → `GOUGH ORDERS THE ATTACK.`

segments.voice: The Sikh army had chosen its ground well: behind cover, guns ready. The scrub broke up the British lines. Units lost touch with each other, and some charged straight into fire they couldn't see until it hit them. The fighting was close and bloody. British accounts describe regiments cut up, guns lost, and men falling back in confusion. On the Sikh side, an army that had lost at Sobraon, and seen land lost at the treaty table, fought hard and gave little away. Night came down on a field nobody had clearly won. The British held part of the ground and claimed the day. The Sikh army drew back in good order, still an army, still ready to fight. In Britain the news landed as a shock, and a new commander was sent out to replace Gough. In the Guru Granth Sahib, a salok of Bhagat Kabir says the true hero is the one who fights for the helpless (some read it, for the faith), and who, even cut to pieces, never leaves the field. In Sikh tellings, Chillianwala is that kind of day: no throne won, nothing changed on the map, but an army that stood its ground. Look back at the week: a kingdom's close and the first war, Sobraon and the treaty, the queen sent away, the spark at Multan. Each day, something taken. Today, something kept.
screen: `A STRONG POSITION IN THE SCRUB.` · `CLOSE, BLOODY FIGHTING.` · `NIGHT, AND NO CLEAR WINNER.` · `THE HERO NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · then, large: `THEY HELD.`

segments.voice: Sit with both feet flat on the floor and feel the ground under them, then bring to mind one place where you usually give way when you'd rather not: a conversation where you go quiet, a habit that wins every evening, a pressure at work. You don't have to fight it now; just feel your feet, and picture yourself, next time, staying where you are for one breath longer. If you pray, let Waheguru be the word on each breath out.
Chillianwala. A battle in thick scrub near the Jhelum, fought into the dark, with no clear winner and a Sikh army that held its ground. Today's word.
Your line: they held. No throne won, and still they stood their ground. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikh histories and tellings remember Chillianwala as a battle where the Khalsa army stood its ground against the British, and the story is told with pride alongside the losses that followed.

notes: No year in the voice (the index title gives 1849). Week-end look back covers days 932–937.
Gough 'had meant to wait for morning' and attacked late in the day follows common accounts; confirm.
'A new commander was sent out to replace Gough' (Charles Napier) is stated without names or dates; confirm wording.
Kabir's verse (soora so pahichaaneeai jo larai deen ke het, purja purja kat marai kabahoo na chhaadai khet) paraphrased; confirm Ang 1105.
Gurmukhi ਸੂਰਾ (soora) should be checked; the verse itself uses ਸੂਰਾ.
Editor: cut 'its guns ... largely intact' from the teach and the myth reveal (some Sikh guns were taken at Chillianwala); the army is now described only as drawing back in good order.
Audit: Kabir's 'deen ke het' is read by some translators as 'for the faith' rather than 'for the helpless'; the voice now names both readings.
